title: Reading List
intro: Books, papers and data for going further, grouped by level. Starred items are the best place to start.

items: ★ *The Little Book of Common Sense Investing*, John C. Bogle: the case for index funds from the man who popularized them.
★ *A Random Walk Down Wall Street*, Burton Malkiel: a lively tour of markets, bubbles and the evidence for indexing; updated many times since 1973.
★ *The Psychology of Money*, Morgan Housel: short essays on behavior, risk and enough.
*The Simple Path to Wealth*, JL Collins: a plain plan for saving and index investing.
*The Bogleheads' Guide to Investing*, Larimore, Lindauer and LeBoeuf; and the Bogleheads wiki, a free, thorough reference.
*If You Can*, William Bernstein: a 16-page pamphlet for young investors, free online.
★ *The Intelligent Investor*, Benjamin Graham (read the edition with Jason Zweig's commentary): margin of safety and the investor's temperament.
*The Four Pillars of Investing*, William Bernstein: theory, history, psychology and business, with portfolios.
*Your Money and Your Brain*, Jason Zweig; *Thinking, Fast and Slow*, Daniel Kahneman.
*Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits*, Philip Fisher; Warren Buffett's letters to Berkshire Hathaway shareholders (free online).
*Stocks for the Long Run*, Jeremy Siegel: two centuries of US returns.
*Triumph of the Optimists*, Dimson, Marsh and Staunton: returns across countries since 1900.
*Manias, Panics, and Crashes*, Charles Kindleberger; *This Time Is Different*, Reinhart and Rogoff: the history of bubbles and financial crises.
*The Most Important Thing*, Howard Marks, and his memos (free online): risk, cycles and second-level thinking.
★ *Investment Valuation* and *The Little Book of Valuation*, Aswath Damodaran, with his free NYU lectures and datasets.
*Valuation: Measuring and Managing the Value of Companies*, McKinsey (Koller, Goedhart and Wessels).
*Expectations Investing*, Mauboussin and Rappaport: reverse DCF.
*Financial Shenanigans*, Howard Schilit: accounting red flags.
*Bond Markets, Analysis, and Strategies*, Frank Fabozzi.
★ *Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives*, John Hull: the standard text, with the mathematics made accessible.
*Option Volatility and Pricing*, Sheldon Natenberg: how option traders think.
*Currency Strategy*, Callum Henderson; the BIS Triennial Survey reports for how the FX market works.
★ *Investments*, Bodie, Kane and Marcus: the standard university textbook covering most of this topic.
*Asset Pricing*, John Cochrane; *Expected Returns*, Antti Ilmanen; *Your Complete Guide to Factor-Based Investing*, Berkin and Swedroe.
*Advances in Financial Machine Learning*, Marcos López de Prado: backtest overfitting and research process.
*Fooled by Randomness* and *The Black Swan*, Nassim Taleb: luck, fat tails and the limits of models.
Markowitz (1952), 'Portfolio Selection', Journal of Finance.
Sharpe (1964), 'Capital Asset Prices'; Sharpe (1991), 'The Arithmetic of Active Management'.
Black and Scholes (1973), 'The Pricing of Options and Corporate Liabilities'; Merton (1973) and (1974).
Fama (1970), 'Efficient Capital Markets'; Fama and French (1992, 1993, 2015).
Kahneman and Tversky (1979), 'Prospect Theory'.
Shiller (1981), 'Do Stock Prices Move Too Much...?'
Barber and Odean (2000), 'Trading Is Hazardous to Your Wealth'.
Bessembinder (2018), 'Do Stocks Outperform Treasury Bills?'
Bengen (1994), 'Determining Withdrawal Rates Using Historical Data'.
SEC EDGAR (filings), FRED (economic data), TreasuryDirect (US Treasury auctions and savings bonds).
Kenneth French's data library; Robert Shiller's data; Damodaran Online.
Portfolio Visualizer (backtests and factor regressions, used with the cautions on the Research page).
SPIVA scorecards (S&P Dow Jones Indices) on active against passive results.
FINRA BrokerCheck and the SEC's adviser search; the UK FCA register.
